blocks.cap: The embankment on the last night of Obon, lanterns going out on the river

blocks.p: All along the river the sending fires were being lit. There were thousands of them. From the embankment the whole of Kita looked like a city of candles laid out on black cloth. The air smelled of smoke and river water and the sweet burnt sugar of a festival stall somewhere behind the houses. On the near bank the smoke went straight up. On the far bank, the one that was not there, the same smoke went up a degree crooked, and something tall and patient leaned over every fire to warm its hands.
Gin turned from the rail. The Healer smiled at Rei with his brother's mouth.
"You came on time," it said. "I knew you would."

Across the water Kanna-sensei had stopped at the top of the far steps. Behind her the mourners of the Far-Shore Circle stood in a line in their dark clothes. There were thirty-five of them, and each one held a framed photograph against their chest. A husband. A daughter. A boy in a school uniform. Kaito stood at her elbow with his eyes rolled up white.

Rei could feel what the line was. All month the Circle had worked like a battery. Every Saturday, new grief had been gathered and stored in those white rooms in Takinogawa. Tonight it was being spent all at once.

"Uedera-kun," Kanna-sensei called across the river. Her voice was soft, and it carried perfectly. It was the voice of a teacher who had never once had to raise it. "You look so tired. Come and sit with us. There is tea."

The wall shivered. The mourners' grief went into it in one long breath. The seam over the river opened another degree. And the chair at its centre, the cold absence Rei had felt from his own flat, leaned toward the far bank like a flame toward an open window.

Rei understood then what Kishin had come for. It had not come to watch, this time. A Qliphoth does not make a feeling of its own. It takes a seat out from under the one holding it and wears the register like a shell. Kishin had been eating Watanabe's seat for months. Tonight, with the ice at its softest, it meant to take the one seat in the city that had no living holder at all. Then it would stand the Tree of Death up on this side of the wall, with itself at the top.
"There," the Healer said quietly, beside him. "Do you see it now, Rei? That is what I have been waiting for."
Rei did not answer it. He did not look at Kishin either. He turned to his brother and did the one thing in Gin's book that nobody had ever taught him.
He listened.

He did not listen to the voice. He listened under it. Gin's body was loud with two things at once, the way a room is loud when two radios are tuned to stations side by side. One of them was calm and even and very old. It was a long clean note of duty that never changed. The other was ragged and frightened and tired and very nearly drowned. And it was humming, under its breath, a song from an old film about a cat bus. They had watched that film together on a borrowed television when Rei was seven.

Finding one consciousness inside a possessed body, as one voice is found in a crowd. That was what Gin's book called Frequency Isolation. Rei had never done it. But he had done the thing underneath it every day of his life without a name for it, sitting in rooms where people were lying to him and hearing the lie. He set everything else aside. The fires. The mourners. The chair. He followed the humming down through the old even note, the way he would have followed his brother's voice through the rush-hour crowd at Ōji station. When he was close enough, he spoke to it directly.
"Gin," he said. "I'm here."
The humming stopped. Under the calm face, something turned its head. Rei felt his brother see him from inside, very small and very far away and completely awake.
Then Rei looked up into the Healer's eyes, and said its name.

He did not say it like an accusation. On the walk down he had thought he would. Now he found that he could not. This thing had worn his brother for a month, and it had kept him alive while it did. It had mended a cut on Gin's hand in the second week that should have needed stitches. It had made the tea. So Rei said the name the way a family thanks a doctor at the end of a long night on a hospital ward, when he is still in his coat and they are still in their chairs and nobody has slept.
"Tachibana Yushiro."

The name did not break it. Tanizaki had been right. The name held it. Rei watched it land. He watched the old even note in his brother's body go still in a new way, the way a hand goes still when someone else's hand is laid over it. The Healer did not leave. It could not leave. It was anchored, held in place in the light by the one person its vessel loved. And for the first time in forty years, someone was calling it by its own name and meant it kindly.

Something in Gin's face changed. It was not the Healer going. It was the Healer staying, and his brother coming up beside it. For a moment both were there at once, and neither had to hide. Gin's eyes. The Healer's stillness. One face.
"Ah," it said, very softly. It sounded almost relieved. "There it is. Nobody has said that in a long time."
"Tell me the truth," Rei said. "All of it. You can't do anything else now."

blocks.cap: Tachibana Yushiro, the Healer, speaking with Gin's face

blocks.p: "I never wanted your chair," Tachibana Yushiro said.
It said it simply, in Gin's voice, the way a doctor gives a diagnosis.

"I died with my hands in a ward full of people who would otherwise have been left. I would not leave them. That is all I am. On the far side there is a seat for what I am. It has stood empty as long as yours has. I mean to take it, and sit in it, and keep it beside the few of my kind I would trust to sit near me. I have no wish to rule the living. I have had my life." It looked across the river. "That one has a different wish. That one means to rule here. To stand the dead tree up on your side of the wall and sit at its crown and keep the living as its harvest. It cannot do that while your chair is filled. And it cannot be killed on this side except by one of us from inside a body. I needed a body. I needed the thin night, so that it would come to the chair in person. And I needed one of you in the chair when it was over."
"Why?" Rei asked. "If you didn't want it."

"Because I am a doctor, Rei." The Healer smiled with Gin's mouth, and it was a tired, real smile. "A doctor does not walk off a ward with no one on duty. I could not go to my seat and leave this district with an empty chair and a thinning wall and the dead coming home every summer to a place that could not tell them apart from the living. Someone had to be on duty here. One of you was always going to fit. I did not much mind which. That is the cruelty you saw in me. It is true. I am sorry for it."
Inside, Gin was listening. Rei could feel him there, awake, watching the thing in him explain itself, the way he had been watching it work for a month.
"Let me do it now," the Healer said. "It is coming. Your brother's body is the only knife on this side of the water. I will be quick with it. I will try to give him back."
Across the river Kanna-sensei began to walk down the far steps toward the water. The mourners came after her. The seam bent toward them like a bow.
"No," Rei said. "Nobody gets spent tonight. Not him. Not anyone."

He went down to the edge of the gravel, where the near bank met the doubled water. He did not look at Kishin. He looked down. Through the river. Through the wall. All the way to the centre, where a tired young man in an old coat stood with his back to the world and his arms around a door.
Rei had six lines written on the back of a registry page. He did not need to read them.
"Your name is Kuze Kaname," he said.

Nothing happened. Then something at the very bottom of the light went still. It went still the way a man stops in the street when he hears someone call a name he has not answered to since he was a child.

"You were born in Edo. You worked for the Twilight Office. Ōmagatoki. You were an investigator. You went out at dusk and looked into what came through." Rei's voice shook, and he let it. "You wouldn't stand on either side of any line. You walked the middle way. You walked it so far you opened every path and every register at once, and there was nothing left of you that was only one thing. And then you sat down in the Duty seat. You became it. You've been holding it for six years on top of everything else, because nobody living came to take it off you."
He took a breath that hurt.

"You answered me once. I asked you what you were holding. You said, the seat I became. My brother said the chair didn't need a new occupant. It needed its old one. He meant you. You're the old one. You never left. You just forgot you were sitting in it."
Down at the centre of the light, the man turned around.
For one terrible interval, nobody held the wall.

Rei felt it go. It was not a tearing. It was a letting go, the way a held breath goes out of a body all at once. The veil fell. The two cities slid together and were one city. Every fire on both banks became a single fire. And every dead person in Kita who had come home for the festival was suddenly standing on the streets among the living, where anyone could see them, bewildered and lit from below.
And behind each of the twelve holders, all across Tokyo, a shell rose up.

Rei saw them all at once, because for that interval there was no distance in the city at all. There were thirteen hollow things, each one in the shape of a single feeling at its worst. Each one turned toward a living person who held the same feeling at its best. Two trees with the same fruit. And the living ones, the light ones, felt them come.

In a public bath in Kita, a man of forty-eight set down his shovel at the boiler door. Mori Takao had held Rage for twenty years, and the others deferred to him. He straightened his back. His voice did not travel through the air. It travelled through the seats. Hold, he said, the eldest, and every one of them heard him.
They held.

In a tea house in Kyoto, Asakura Mio put down a cup and kept Grief open and steady with both hands. In a quiet office Sakuma Kei held Love. Nakashima Yuna held Fear at the top of her stairwell, with Okabe Natsumi beside her holding Courage, the two of them linked as they had been for twelve years. Chen Lian held Wonder among the Grid's oldest books. On Sakae Street, Hoshino Haru held Joy over a pot of broth that had been on the stove for eight hours. Kobayashi Emi held Shame. Inoue Satoru stopped walking for the first time in three years and held Hunger standing still. In a room behind a restaurant in Shin-Ōkubo, Park Junho held Longing on his feet, and through the paper door the whole front room was singing. Somewhere in the city Kasumi Shin opened an old book to its first page and held Awe. He was the closest of them all to the man at the centre, who had just turned around.

In Itabashi, in a cardigan two sizes too big, Watanabe Jun held Despair. The shell that rose behind him was not a stranger. It had a teacher's soft face. It had been eating his seat for months. Now it reached for him with both hands.

Thirteen light anchors against thirteen shells. But only twelve of the anchors were lit. The thirteenth seat stood open in the middle of the city like a door, and Kishin's whole weight was leaning toward it.
Rei took the chair.

He did not take it as a throne. He took it as a duty. It was his own register, the one his family had buried in him before he could read. The one Gin had taught him to hide at a kitchen table as a trick for sleeping. The one that did not change because it did not need to. He did not feed the hungry grain in his palms. He did not take anyone's feeling to make himself strong. He opened the single unchanging thing he had always been, and he held it, sane and willing, with himself.
It was heavier than anything he had ever carried. It was also, to his astonishment, familiar. It was the weight of getting up every morning for a brother who did not come home.
Thirteen.
The moment the last seat lit, the shells had nothing to wear.

A Qliphoth lives by taking an anchor out from under a holder. Thirteen holders, every one of them alive and willing, left no empty seat to climb into. Light anchors can kill demons. Demons can only possess anchors. With every anchor lit, the shells stood in the falling veil like coats with no one inside them.
Kishin did not stand still. It came across the water.

It came in Fukai Rinka's body, walking on the river as if the river were a floor, and despair came with it like weather. Rei felt it hit the bank. Every person on the embankment sat down where they stood. On the far side the mourners dropped their photographs. The despair was aimed at the chair, and at Rei sitting in it. It was the strongest thing he had ever felt. It was a soft voice saying none of it matters, none of it ever did, sit, rest, drink the tea.
Gin's hands moved.

Right thumb on the left knuckles, one, three, two. The heel of the hand flat on the breastbone. Fingers steepled. Rei saw it and knew it and could have wept. The keys. Under the grey cardigan, the binding on his brother's forearm had been loaded and waiting for six years at a low hum. Now it fired at full strength. The Healer did not stop him. The Healer added its own weight to it. Two of them in one body, the man and the doctor, threw one binding across the gravel together.
It caught Kishin at the water's edge and held it for a breath.

Rei had his hand in the kit bag. Restraining Circle, the second sleeve, drawn on a Monday morning with forty sheets of Kanda washi on the desk. He slapped it down on the wet stones at the edge of the river and felt it fire, with Gin's precision and his own rank behind it. It would not hold a thing like Kishin for long. Gin's book had said so. Against the strongest, every configuration only bought time.
Time was all they needed.

In Itabashi, Watanabe Jun felt the hands on his seat loosen. He was thirty-five and looked fifty and had tried to retire three times. Never in his life had he been less alone in Despair than he was in that interval, with eleven others holding beside him and a new one in the thirteenth seat. He took hold of his own register with both hands and pulled it back. The shell tore off his seat like wet paper.
Kishin screamed.

With the veil fallen, everyone saw it. Rei had not understood that until it happened. There was no wall to hide behind. Thirty-five mourners on the far bank looked at their gentle teacher and saw what was wearing her. The despair register with nothing left to hold. A shape like a coat over a coat, the dead woman's soft face slipping on something that had never had a face. On the bridge above the north stretch of the river, a young man in a paint-stained shirt stood with three phones held up in a fan in front of him. He was filming, and crying, and not stopping. Itsuki. Rei had told him where to stand.

Kishin fled. It went back into Fukai Rinka's body the way a hand goes back into a pocket. It turned, and it ran, and the despair went out of the air behind it like a tide going out. On the far steps Kaito sat down hard, blinking. He started to cry like a boy who has woken from a fever and does not know where he is. He was alive. All of them were alive. The Circle's photographs lay on the steps, and the mourners were picking them up, one by one, and looking at them as if for the first time.

blocks.cap: Rei and Kuze Kaname face to face at the centre

blocks.p: When Rei looked down again, the man at the centre was looking back at him.

Kuze Kaname had his name back. It sat on him oddly, like a coat taken out of the cupboard after a long winter. He was very young. He looked at Rei in the thirteenth seat, and Rei understood, without any words passing between them, that he was being thanked. He was being thanked by a man who had not been allowed to put anything down since the Edo period.
You took the weight, he said. It was the first sentence he had spoken in his own voice in a very long time. He said it carefully, as if checking that his voice still worked.
"Some of it," Rei said. "You're still holding the rest. Can you hold it as you? Not as the chair?"

Kaname thought about this with the serious attention of an investigator turning over a piece of evidence. Then he turned back to the wall. But he did not stand as he had stood before, with his back to the world and his whole self gone into the holding. He turned like a man going back to work after a night's sleep. With his name on.
The veil came back.

It came back held by living hands, thirteen of them, and by one man at the centre who was a person again. The two cities slid apart into their proper places. The dead stood a moment longer among the fires. Then they turned and went down to the river, following the smoke home, the way they were meant to. The seam over the Arakawa closed along its whole length like a healed cut. It left only a faint bright line on the water. Rei somehow knew that line would still be there every August.

Rei sat in the chair, and the chair was a weight, and the weight was his. He did not become a weather with a person left over. He was a person carrying a weather. It was not the same thing. He could feel the difference the way Park Junho had felt it, standing.
The Axis, mostly light now, stood with him.
Gin was sitting on the gravel against the rail with his knees drawn up. The Healer was still in him, still anchored, still looking out of his eyes with that serious, tired patience.
"Well," it said. "There is someone on duty."
"There's someone on duty," Rei agreed.

"And the other one is seen. Running. It will not stand the dead tree up on this side now, with every seat lit and a living tree in the way." The Healer was quiet for a moment. "I wanted it dead. I thought that was the only way to be sure. You have shown me another. I do not have to like it."

"No," Rei said. "Your seat's still there. On the other side. Go and take it. Sit with the ones you trust. Keep that one from climbing over there, if you can. That's a duty too. You don't need him for it." He crouched down in front of his brother. "Please. Give him back."

He took the two washi bundles out of his jacket and untied the first. Inside were four outer glyphs and a centre mark. Each had its compass position pencilled on the back in Gin's hand. Rei laid them out on the wet gravel around his brother. North, east, south, west. Gin had prepared three sets of this circle. He had used one, once, in six years, after three months of preparation, and it had worked. The circle fired when all five pieces touched the ground, the centre last. Rei felt it close around his brother like cupped hands. It was not made to banish. Gin's book said the entity inside could not jump to a new host. It could only go deeper, or leave through the open top of the circle.
It was a door. Not a tear. A door, with someone holding it open politely.
Tachibana Yushiro looked at the circle, and at Rei, and something like amusement crossed his brother's face.
"You are offering me the way out instead of throwing me through it," it said. "That is a physician's manners. Where did you learn them?"
"From you," Rei said. "You made the tea."
The Healer laughed. It was Gin's laugh, quiet and surprised. Then it laid Gin's hand flat on Gin's own chest for a moment, over the heart, the way a doctor checks a patient before he signs him out.

"He is very tired," it said. "Feed him. Let him sleep longer than he wants to. He will not be the same as the man who went in. Time inside does things. But he is there, and he is watching you, and he has been proud of you the whole time. I have heard him."

It went up and out through the open top of the circle, toward a seat on the far side that had waited for it as long as Rei's had. Rei felt it go. It did not feel like an exorcism. It felt like a man in a white coat walking out of a ward at dawn, after handing over his notes.
Gin fell forward into Rei's arms.

He weighed nothing. He weighed everything. He was cold and shaking, and he smelled of the cardigan and the river and himself. After a long time he said, into Rei's shoulder, in a voice that had not been used properly for a month, "You burned it. The one in the drawer."
"Yes."
"Good," Gin said. "I didn't want it."
Up on the far embankment, the first light came.

Kishin was exposed by morning. Itsuki's footage could not show what a camera cannot see. But it showed thirty-five people dropping their photographs at the same moment and backing away from a woman in a pale cardigan, and that was enough to start a file. Higuchi's ledger and Gin's book did the rest. The Far-Shore Circle's house in Takinogawa was found empty. The white rooms were bare. The wall of photographs of the missing was still up. Very quietly, the CVD began to hunt a woman who had been marked alive in an old file. Watanabe Jun slept for eleven hours.

A week later Rei went to meet Okada Shizuka. Obon was over. The lanterns had come down from the doorsteps, and the trains were full again of people coming back from their family graves in the country, with paper bags of local sweets for the office and sunburn on the backs of their necks. Rei walked to Higashi-Jūjō and rode the sky-blue Keihin-Tōhoku line one stop to Ōji. The cicadas in Asukayama were as loud as ever. It was still thirty-three degrees.

Okada was waiting in the back booth of Café Mikazuki. It was two floors above the street near the ward office, and the booth sat in a small dead spot where nobody's register could be read. The owner, Maruyama, brought two coffees and went away without being asked. Okada had a second file with her. It was the draft of the Closing, the Office of Public Confidence's plan to catalogue every medium in the city and seal the axis shut. Rei had seen what the axis was now. He had talked to him.

"Adachi read both files last night," Okada said. "He sat with them for an hour. Then he told me something he has never told anyone. He has known about the Thirteen for twelve years. He met one of them, once, and it retired him from the field. And two years ago he assessed your brother's real rank, in a corridor, in the time it takes to say good morning. He knew exactly what Gin was. He let the suppression run because he thought Gin was safer hidden." She turned her cup on its saucer. "He said he should have gone to him eighteen months ago. He said that twice."
"Where are the files now?"
"On the President's desk," Okada said. "He took them up himself this morning."

The Director of the Office of Public Confidence was not dismissed. That was not how things were done. She was buried instead. She was buried under the proof, under an inquiry, under a quiet line in the budget that was moved somewhere else. For a while her glass office in Marunouchi was still lit at night, with the radio on. Then one week it was not.
Rei lived an ordinary life in Tokyo after that. He also channelled something vast. Both things were true, and the tension between them did not resolve. After a while he stopped needing it to.

Most mornings he was up at five, because Duty got up early. At that hour the ward was blue and quiet. The first trains were starting to run, and their station jingles carried a long way in the empty streets. Crows argued on the rubbish nets. A man in white gloves was hosing down the pavement in front of a pachinko parlour that would not open for hours. Rei walked to the Akebono Bakery by the station, on the night-bus route, just as it opened. Mrs. Kawai sold him an an-pan, a soft bun filled with sweet red bean paste, without asking what he wanted. He sat by the window until it stopped, whatever it was that morning. The weight settling. The city's long, unchanging hum of things people kept doing because stopping would cost too much. Sometimes it took ten minutes. Sometimes a stranger sat down at the next table who carried Love for a living, or Joy, and nodded at him, and said nothing, and they ate their bread together.

When Gin was strong enough to walk that far, the two of them warded the dead market arcade. Gin talked him through every fold. Rei drew the Purification set himself, badly the first time and well the second, under Tanizaki's eye, on a floor with faint chalk ghosts on it. They placed the set on a Sunday when the shutters were down. Over the next weeks the man in the flat above the arcade began to sleep through the night. He was Mr. Tachibana, a salaryman nobody would ever look at twice. His face lost its grey. He bought new plants for the windowsill. He never learned why he had nearly not recovered. Rei did not tell him that his name was the name of a doctor. It was a common name. It had only been a coincidence. Rei had started to like coincidences again.

Mrs. Okuma taught him to light a lantern properly, both the bad-anniversary lantern and the ordinary kind. She came down to the memorial every evening to see whether he was doing it right. He never quite was. So she had to keep coming. By the next March she had stopped talking about the river as a place she was going.

blocks.cap: Mr. Kishi, who never left Tsuru-no-yu

blocks.p: He went to Tsuru-no-yu at last, the way Gin had been telling him to for years. It was the old public bath behind the market, under a tall brick chimney. In the changing room the floor was made of polished wood boards, and a fan turned slowly under the ceiling. Mrs. Hara looked up from the high desk where she took the money and said, "Mind the step." Then she said to the empty bench by the far tub, "That's the younger one, Kishi-san. Finally."

The far tub was warm with no fire under it. Mr. Kishi had soaked there for forty years. He died in 2009, the same year the thirteenth seat went empty, and he simply stayed. Mrs. Hara was seventy-one. She kept a list of every dead person in the ward and the corner each one had died on. She meant to teach it to one person before she went, so that whoever kept Mr. Kishi company after her would know who he was talking to. She had chosen Rei. He came on Tuesdays.

blocks.cap: The child in the empty seat at the Suzuran

blocks.p: One night, unable to sleep with the weight, he went out at two in the morning. The streets were empty. The vending machines on the corners glowed and hummed to nobody. A taxi went by slowly with its red light on, looking for a fare. He walked into the Suzuran, the little bar pressed up against the worst of the ward's thin spots. A cat slept on the till there, and the rule was that nobody pointed at it.

A woman with long ash-grey hair sat at the back in the same coat she wore in every season. She was murmuring to the empty seat beside her. A child sat in it. Only she could see him. Only she, and now Rei. Beside her, nursing a whisky somebody had bought him, sat Sugimoto Hiroshi, the homeless professor, the one person she would talk to.

Rei did not try to clear anything. He sat with the two of them until four, and listened. The second time he came, Sugimoto had got her to say it out loud. There had been a fire, years ago. She had been the neighbour who got out. The thing that needed releasing had never been the child. It was her guilt. It took a month. Then one night the seat beside her was empty, and she went home. The next evening the barman said she had not come in. Rei hoped with his whole heart that it was because she was asleep.

blocks.cap: Leo's teacher, the voice in the club mirror

blocks.p: He went back to Shin-Ōkubo on a Thursday. He took the green Saikyō line from Jūjō down to Shinjuku and changed to the Yamanote line for one stop.

The narrow main street of Shin-Ōkubo was packed, as it always was, with teenage girls hunting for posters of their favourite singers, with the smell of grilled meat and spicy rice cakes, and with music pouring out of every shop door. He went to Park Junho's class at the community centre first. Afterwards he went to Eomma's, and he found the young man in the good suit eating ramyeon alone at the corner table again.

His working name was Leo. His real name was Sato. Rei sat down across from him and told him what he was. A medium, untrained and unregistered, who read the room at the club with a gift he had always called intuition. And Rei told him that the voice he sometimes heard in the mirror before a hard table was real. It was a man who had loved him and taught him the trade and wanted him out of it before it ate him too. Leo cried into his noodles, very elegantly. The next time Rei passed the black window at the corner table, there was only one face in it.

And he went back to the north bridge, as he had promised. Nagai Haruto was there with his river stone, keeping the others back from the edge. Rei sat on the steps beside him and asked him, quietly, who he talked to downstream. The boy went very still. Then he told him. The small drowned boy in the shallows had been keeping the same watch for years. Rei told Haruto there was a Grid that would teach him what he was before the CVD found him. He told him that the boy downstream had been doing, for free, all this time, exactly the work the institution said only it could do. Haruto turned the stone over twice in his pocket. Then he said he would think about it. That was how Rei knew he would.

blocks.cap: Rei and Gin on a night out in the city

blocks.p: Gin cooked for three again.

It took him a long time to come back. He was not the man who went in. He was slower. He forgot things, and the forgetting frightened him. Some mornings he stood at the cooker with the pan in his hand and could not remember what he had meant to make. Rei would say curry or the egg thing, and Gin would say yes, as if Rei had handed him back a word. He did not wear the grey cardigan again. He threw it out himself. But he was there. He wrote again, in a hand that stood upright. Sometimes in the evenings he read aloud from the archive in a voice that was entirely his own. If anything in him leaned, Rei never felt it.

Daiki came round on the first Friday Gin was well enough to have people. Sasaki Daiki lived two stops away on the line. He was Rei's oldest friend. He had kept texting all month without ever getting a straight answer, and he had never once stopped. He sat down at the kitchen table where the kettle had gone cold on the first morning. Gin put a plate in front of him, and Daiki ate like he had been starving. He had been, a little. He had been worried. He did not ask what had happened. He asked for seconds.

Tanizaki came on the Sunday. He brought his own tea, because he did not trust theirs. He made it the old way at their table and poured three cups. He pushed one across to each brother and kept the third for himself. Nobody had gone. There was no cup for the absent. He drank, and watched Gin over the rim, and watched Rei, and he did not say anything about it.

That night, after Gin had gone to bed, Rei sat at the desk under the lamp with the archive open in front of him. There was one chapter Gin had never finished. Chapter Fourteen. It was a guide to finding the frequency of a domain anchor, written for someone who would need it. Gin had written it for Rei. Rei picked up the pen and began to finish it, in Gin's format, in his own bad hand.

When he had done the first page he signed it the way Gin signed everything. Then he got up and went to the genkan, and hung both sets of keys on the hook by the door. His and his brother's. Side by side.
R.U. Keys on the hook.
